To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of cancer in the Boehringer cohort is significantly elevated (pooled SMR=1.16, 95% confidence intervals 1.04-1.29), that the risk is significantly increased for cancers of the lung, lymphatic and hematopoeitic system, buccal cavity, pharynx, and non-Hodgkins lymphoma, and that the risk is not increased for cancers of stomach, colon, rectum, pancreas, prostate, testis

(a) there is a positive dose-response relationship for all cancers combined and for cancers of the respiratory system, and (b) the risk of lung cancer increases with increasing duration of employment and with increasing cumulative exposure to dioxins.

the risk of lung cancer was 1.5-fold higher among workers with high exposure to phenoxy acid herbicides and chlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans, and that the risk of lymphatic and hematopoeitic cancer was 2.7-fold higher among workers who were highly exposed to phenoxy acids and chlorinated dibenzofuranes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms by which chemicals induce cancer and with the development of methods to estimate risks to human health from exposures to environmental chemicals.
the effects of dioxin and related compounds on humans.
the development and application of mathematical models for the analysis of epidemiologic and toxicologic data, with the objective of improving our ability to estimate human cancer risks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dioxins are carcinogens, but the evidence is not sufficient to quantify the risk of specific types of cancer.

dioxin and related chemicals are carcinogenic in animals, but their carcinogenicity in humans has not been established, and that epidemiologic research on workers has yielded some, but not conclusive evidence of excess cancer in exposed groups.
dioxin and dioxinlike compounds have been demonstrated to be animal carcinogens, that they may cause cancer in humans, but that the risk is probably low.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dioxin and dioxinlike compounds have not been conclusively shown to cause cancer in humans, and that the available evidence is not sufficient to rule out a causal role for cancer.
dioxin is not a major human carcinogen, but the data are too limited to rule it out as such.

the results are compatible with a small increase in risk of cancer in dioxin and dioxinlike compound-exposed workers, with the excesses being limited to lymphatic and hematologic malignancies and to respiratory cancers in workers with the highest exposure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a lot of variation in the risk for developing cancer from exposure to dioxins and dixinlike compounds.
there is a lot of variation in how people experience their cancer.
the dioxin-like chemicals in the environment are not causing cancer in humans.
